why: Comparing a burr, a sideways pull and a peel helps your child explain how many tiny hooks and loops share one strong grip.
teaser: Hear a strap rip, meet the burr that started it, then test why a sideways pull holds but a peel lets go.
title: How Velcro Works
question: How can two soft strips of cloth hold on so tightly, then rip open?
idea: Hook and loop copies a burr. Stiff nylon hooks on one strip catch soft loops on the other. One hook is weak, but hundreds share a sideways pull. A peel opens just a few hooks at a time, so it lets go easily.

curiosity.intro: Start with a shoe strap that rips. Then follow it back to a burr on a walk, look at hooks and loops up close, and test a pull against a peel.
curiosity.carryForward: Next time a strap rips open, listen: how many tiny hooks just let go?

questions.question: Where did the idea come from?
questions.notice: Find the tiny hooks at the tips of the burr's spines.
questions.say: A burr. In 1941, a Swiss engineer came home from a walk with burdock burrs stuck to his socks and his dog's fur. Under a microscope, each spine ended in a tiny hook. Burrs cling on purpose: animals carry their seeds to new places.
questions.try: After a walk outdoors, look closely at your socks. Did any seeds hitch a ride? Look at one with a magnifying glass for hooks.

questions.question: How do you make a tiny hook?
questions.notice: Compare the stiff hooks on top with the soft loops below.
questions.say: You start with a loop. The first hooks were cotton and wore out. Nylon worked better: it was woven into loops, heated so the loops kept their shape, then a cutter snipped one side of each loop to leave a hook.
questions.try: Bend a pipe cleaner into a small loop. Open one side a little so it becomes a hook. Can your hook catch a loop of yarn?

questions.question: Why does a peel open so easily?
questions.notice: Look at how thin the line is where the strip is letting go.
questions.say: A sideways pull, called shear, makes every hook hold at once. A peel opens only one thin line of hooks at a time. The rrrip is hooks springing free, one row after another.
questions.try: Press two strips together. Slide them apart sideways, then peel one corner. Which one takes less push? Listen to each.

questions.question: Why do old strips lose their grip?
questions.notice: Find the fuzz in the hooks and the clean part next to it.
questions.say: Lint and fluff pack into the hooks, so they cannot reach the loops. A fine comb can lift the fuzz out, and the grip comes back.
questions.try: Find a fuzzy strip on an old shoe or bag. Comb it gently with an old comb or toothbrush, then test the grip again.

beats.title: A burr on a walk
beats.passage: In 1941, a Swiss engineer went for a walk with his dog. Afterward, burdock burrs clung to his socks and the dog's fur. He looked at a burr under a microscope. Each spine ended in a tiny hook. The hooks caught on loops of thread and fur. Could cloth copy that trick?
beats.prompt: What did the engineer see under the microscope?

beats.title: Hooks meet loops
beats.passage: Look very closely at the two sides. The rough side holds rows of stiff little hooks, like tiny bent canes. The soft side is a fuzzy tangle of thread loops. Press them together, and hundreds of hooks catch hundreds of loops. One hook is weak, but many together are strong. The name Velcro mixes French words for velvet and hook.
beats.prompt: Why is one hook weak but many hooks strong?

foldable.heading: Hooks meet loops
foldable.body: Stiff hooks on one side catch soft loops on the other. One hook is weak, but hundreds together hold strong.

beats.title: Pull or peel?
beats.passage: Try pulling the two sides apart sideways, like sliding. It is very hard, because every hook pulls at the same time. Now peel back one corner. It opens easily, because only one thin line of hooks lets go at a time. The rrrip is hooks springing free, row after row. A sideways pull is called shear.
beats.prompt: Why is a peel easier than a sideways pull?

foldable.heading: Pull or peel?
foldable.body: A sideways pull is hard, because every hook pulls at once. A peel is easy: only one thin line lets go.

beats.title: A bag that hangs
beats.passage: A strip on a little board holds a small cloth bag. Big Wonderer points at it. The bag pulls straight down along the strip, so all the hooks share the load, and nothing slips. Then Little Wonderer reaches up and peels one corner. Rrrip! A few hooks at a time let go, and the bag slides off.
beats.prompt: Why does the bag hang without slipping?

foldable.heading: A bag that hangs
foldable.body: A hanging bag pulls along the strip, so every hook shares the weight. Peel one corner, and the bag slides off.

beats.title: When grip fades
beats.passage: Making the hooks took years of trying. The inventor wove nylon loops, heated them to set their shape, then snipped one side of each loop to leave a hook. After many uses, lint fills the hooks, so they cannot reach the loops. A fine comb can lift the fuzz out. Why would a cleaner strip grip better?
beats.prompt: Why does an old strip full of lint grip less?

foldable.heading: When grip fades
foldable.body: Nylon loops were heated, then snipped into hooks. Lint clogs old hooks, but a fine comb can lift it out.

beats.passage: In 1941, a Swiss engineer came home from a walk in the hills with his dog and found burdock burrs clinging stubbornly to his wool socks and to the dog's fur. Burrs cling like this on purpose, so that passing animals carry their seeds to new places. Curious, he looked at a burr under a microscope and saw that every spine ended in a tiny curved hook. Those hooks snagged on loops of thread and tangles of fur, and he wondered whether two strips of cloth could copy the trick.
beats.prompt: How did a plant's way of spreading seeds become an invention?

beats.passage: Seen up close, the rough side holds neat rows of stiff nylon hooks, each bent like a tiny walking cane, while the soft side is a fuzzy tangle of thread loops. When the two sides are pressed together, hundreds of hooks catch hundreds of loops at the same moment. A single hook is weak and slips free easily, but when hundreds share the work, the grip becomes surprisingly strong. The name Velcro joins the first sounds of two French words, velours for velvet and crochet for hook.
beats.prompt: Why does sharing the work make the grip strong?

beats.passage: Pulling the two sides apart sideways, as if sliding one strip along the other, is surprisingly hard, because every hook resists at the same time. Engineers call that kind of sliding force shear, and hook-and-loop strips are strongest against it. Peeling back a corner is easy, because only a thin line of hooks has to let go at any moment while the rest wait their turn. The rrrip you hear is the sound of hooks springing free from their loops, one row after another.
beats.prompt: Why is a strip strong against shear but weak against a peel?

beats.passage: A strip stuck to a small board held a cloth bag that hung straight down without slipping at all. Big Wonderer explained that the bag pulled along the strip, so every hook shared its weight in shear. Then Little Wonderer reached up and peeled one corner instead. With a rrrip, the hooks let go a few at a time until the bag slid off into waiting mittens. The same strip held firmly or opened easily depending only on the direction of the pull.
beats.prompt: How does the direction of a pull change what the strip does?

beats.passage: Making the hooks turned out to be the hardest part of the invention. It took years of trying. Early cotton hooks were too soft and wore out, so the inventor switched to nylon, which keeps its shape after heating. Nylon thread was woven into loops and heat-set, and then a cutter like a barber's clippers snipped one side of each loop to leave a hook. After many uses, lint and fluff pack into the hooks so they cannot reach the loops. Why might combing out the lint bring the grip back?
beats.prompt: How were the loops turned into hooks?

poem.title: A Thousand Tiny Hands
lines: Little Wonderer opened a strap on a shoe,
and it went RRRIP! like a grumpy kazoo.
“Who’s hiding in there?” asked the small one, aghast.
“A thousand tiny hands,” said the big one, “holding fast.”
One side is all hooks, like a crowd of bent canes,
or umbrellas turned upside down, left out in the rains.
The other side’s loops, like a soft curly mat,
and the hooks grab the loops, and that’s simply that.
Big Wonderer said, “Slide them sideways — they’ll hold,
every hook pulling hard, all together and bold.
But peel from a corner, a few at a time,
and they let go as easy as saying this rhyme.”
Who dreamed it up first? Not a wizard or king,
but a burr on a dog, such a scratchy small thing.
So the little one bowed to a burr on its stem:
“Thank you for holding on. We learned it from them.”
